title: The Vow of Junebug Creek
premise: When pastry chef Ines Marchetti inherits a half-share of Junebug Creek Orchard, he discovers the other name on the deed belongs to Teo Alvarado—the man who vanished from his life eleven years ago and took the truth of why with him. Forced to co-own the failing orchard through one growing season, they rebuild an uneasy partnership that deepens into something neither can deny, even as a developer's offer and a buried family secret threaten to tear it apart. At the vineyard's first harvest, Ines must choose between selling out and staying visible, finally letting Teo stay past the last train. They keep the orchard, sign nothing, and begin again in the present tense.
about_author: Jude Villalobos is the pen name of a former line cook who spent six seasons working orchards in the Central Valley before turning to fiction. Their stories explore how people survive what love costs them, and what they find when they stop paying.

chapters.title: Three Missed Payments
chapters.summary: Ines's POV. The café's final notice arrives the same morning as a certified letter: he has inherited half of Junebug Creek Orchard, co-owned with a stranger named Teo Alvarado. Ines recognizes the name and burns his toast, hands shaking. Emotional beat: dread disguised as indifference; the past knocking at a door he bricked over.

chapters.title: The Man Who Left in June
chapters.summary: Flashback woven through Ines's drive to the orchard—eleven years ago, Teo disappeared mid-summer without goodbye, leaving only a note Ines still keeps in a flour tin. Present-day Ines arrives to find the farmhouse half-ruined and a truck already parked outside. Emotional beat: old grief resurfacing as irritation, armor going up.

chapters.title: Co-Signers
chapters.summary: Teo's POV. Teo expected hostility and gets it, but the will's terms are explicit: neither can sell without the other's signature, and the orchard must produce one harvest or revert to the county. He proposes a season-long truce. Ines refuses, then sees the café notice again. Emotional beat: reluctant negotiation; pride losing to arithmetic.

chapters.title: Pruning Season
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. Ines moves into the farmhouse 'temporarily,' insisting he'll handle the books while Teo handles the trees. Their first week is silent warfare—mismatched methods, shared coffee, careful distance. A storm forces them to stake the young vines together through the night. Emotional beat: proximity as slow erosion of anger.

chapters.title: What the Neighbors Know
chapters.summary: Ines's POV. Town gossips fill gaps: Teo came back two years ago, lives alone, bought back his father's debts. Ines learns Teo left eleven years ago right after Ines's father accused him of stealing. Marisol, the feed-store owner, warns Ines gently that some truths were buried for good reasons. Emotional beat: curiosity rekindling into suspicion.

chapters.title: The Developer's Letter
chapters.summary: Teo's POV. A development company offers a sum that would erase both their debts—if both sign within ninety days. Teo hides the letter, then can't. Ines reads it twice and says no before Teo finishes explaining. First real argument in a decade, ending with Ines admitting he doesn't actually want to sell. Emotional beat: conflict revealing alignment beneath it.

chapters.title: Flour and Grafting Wax
chapters.summary: Ines's POV. Ines starts baking in the farmhouse kitchen on weekends, selling out of a roadside stand to fund equipment. Teo starts buying loaves under the pretense of quality control. Small rituals form: Sunday bread, Thursday ledgers, a radio they pretend not to share. Emotional beat: domesticity sneaking in through the side door.

chapters.title: The Accusation, Retold
chapters.summary: Teo's POV. Marisol corners Teo, tells him Ines never believed the theft charge but never asked either. Flashback: Teo's father was the thief; Teo left to protect Ines from the fallout and shame. Teo decides to tell Ines everything, then loses his nerve when Ines laughs at something on the porch. Emotional beat: courage gathering, then faltering.

chapters.title: Blossom Weekend
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. The town's blossom festival brings crowds; the stand sells out; Ines and Teo work shoulder to shoulder until midnight. A festival dance, two glasses of cider, and a kiss interrupted by Ines pulling away—'I don't do this anymore.' Teo says, 'You used to.' Emotional beat: desire breaking surface, fear slamming it shut.

chapters.title: Cold Snap
chapters.summary: Ines's POV. After the almost-kiss, Ines retreats to the café for two weeks, running from himself as much as from Teo. Frost threatens the blossoms; Teo calls once, leaves no message. Ines returns unannounced at dawn to find Teo alone in the rows with smudge pots, exhausted. Emotional beat: avoidance collapsing into tenderness.

chapters.title: The Night the Trains Stopped
chapters.summary: Teo's POV. The freight line through Junebug Creek is being decommissioned; the last train passes in May. Teo tells Ines about the night he left—how he stood at the station, ticket in hand, waiting for Ines to come stop him. Ines never came because Ines's father intercepted the note. Both realize they were robbed, not abandoned. Emotional beat: devastating mutual recognition; grief reframed.

chapters.title: Present Tense
chapters.summary: Ines's POV. For the first time, they speak plainly: what they were, what it cost, what they want now. No promises—Ines can't yet—but honesty instead. They fall into each other carefully, agreeing to let the season decide. Emotional beat: fragile reconciliation; hope handled like ripe fruit.

chapters.title: Set Fruit
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. Early summer: the crop sets heavy, the best in a decade. The developer escalates, pressuring the county and spreading word that the orchard is doomed. Ines's café landlord offers to forgive arrears if Ines signs as the developer's consultant—a trap dressed as rescue. Emotional beat: stakes rising; happiness shadowed by leverage.

chapters.title: The Flour Tin
chapters.summary: Teo's POV. Teo finds Ines's old note in the flour tin—his own handwriting, 'wait for me'—and understands Ines kept faith for eleven years. Meanwhile Ines discovers documents in the farmhouse attic suggesting Teo's father stole not money but the deed itself, defrauding Ines's family. Emotional beat: tenderness on one side, a landmine on the other.

chapters.title: Everything I Didn't Ask
chapters.summary: Ines's POV. Ines confronts Teo with the attic papers: the orchard was never rightfully Alvarado property. Teo knew—he'd been trying to quietly restore the title for two years, which is why he returned. Ines, raw, accuses him of another lie by omission and walks to the station road. Emotional beat: the central wound reopened; loyalty vs. truth made flesh.

chapters.title: Ninety Days
chapters.summary: Teo's POV. With three weeks to harvest and the signing deadline looming, the developer makes a final offer directly to Ines—enough to save the café outright, no strings except silence about the title defect. Ines doesn't answer. Teo files the corrective paperwork anyway, prepared to give Ines the whole orchard. Emotional beat: sacrifice offered without audience.

chapters.title: Last Train Out
chapters.summary: Ines's POV. On the night the final train passes through, Ines stands where Teo stood eleven years ago and finally understands the choice from the other side. He goes home—not to the café, to the orchard—and asks Teo to stay. Not for the harvest. Past the last train. Emotional beat: the blurb's promise fulfilled; choosing presence over escape.

chapters.title: First Pick
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. Harvest begins. The whole town shows up—Marisol, the café regulars, even the skeptical neighbors. Ines bakes with the first fruit; Teo works the rows beside him. The county clerk arrives mid-harvest with the corrected title: joint ownership, clean and legal. Emotional beat: communal joy; the orchard becoming theirs in every sense.

chapters.title: The Signature
chapters.summary: Ines's POV. The developer's lawyer appears at the harvest dinner with a contract and a pen. Ines signs—one line, tearing up the offer publicly, naming the title fraud aloud so it can never be leveraged again. Teo watches him choose visibility over safety. Emotional beat: climax of theme; the price of survival paid in full, gladly.

chapters.title: Cider and Ash
chapters.summary: Teo's POV. Aftermath: the developer retaliates with a nuisance suit, and the café's lease officially dies. Low point after triumph—Ines wonders if he traded everything for a gamble. Teo proposes converting the farmhouse kitchen into the café's new home. Ines says yes before he finishes asking. Emotional beat: grief and rebuilding braided together.

chapters.title: The Vow of Junebug Creek
chapters.summary: Ines's POV. One year later, opening morning of Marchetti-Alvarado at the orchard: a small café, a full counter, their names on the door and the deed. They exchange private vows under the oldest tree—not wedding vows exactly, but close enough. Emotional beat: resolution; identity rebuilt, love in present tense.

chapters.title: After the Harvest
chapters.summary: Dual POV, closing chapter. Late autumn, first frost. Ines locks the café; Teo banks the fire. On the porch, they talk about next year's planting and the past stops feeling like a debt. The last image: the flour tin, now holding a new note—'stayed.' Emotional beat: quiet permanence; the story's themes settled into soil.
